item.title: At COP31, leaders of island countries warn of 'life-or-death' crisis
item.description: Leaders of Seychelles and Niue warned that rising seas and extreme weather threaten the survival of island nations, urging urgent climate action and stronger financial support.
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: Small island leaders on Thursday called for urgent action, describing planet heating as a life-or-death issue for their people at the climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. Alix Sebastien Pillay, the vice president of Seychelles, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, said his country’s very survival was at stake. “It is time to move past the talking,” Pillay said. “For Seychelles, climate action is not simply an environmental priority.” Pillay was speaking on the second day of the leaders’ summit at the UN climate talks, where government leaders addressed the state of a warming world and what they plan to do about it. While the entire globe is threatened by stronger storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and floods, island nations are among the hardest hit by climate change, as they also have to deal with rising seas swallowing up their land. Pillay said Seychelles was experiencing millions of dollars in damage as a result of storms and floods, despite contributing little to increased global warming. He said a UN fund created to compensate for climate-related loss and damage needed to be urgently strengthened. “Climate recovery must not come at the expense of our development or push vulnerable nations further into unsustainable debt.” Speaking at the talks, Dalton Tagelagi, prime minister of the small Pacific island of Niue, said the El Niño conditions that have driven up global temperatures were a warning of what might happen if planet heating was not controlled. “Sea temperatures in the central Pacific are more than three degrees above normal. It is a warning of what is coming if we do not cut emissions now,” Tagelagi said. The comment came as a report said the world had failed to slow global warming trends in the past five years because plans were not realised and efforts that would have helped were cancelled out. “Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions cancelling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report. On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the appointment of a special representative to deal with security risks from the climate crisis, one of the first such appointments anywhere in the world. “Climate is a national security issue,” Burnham said at the summit. Meanwhile, climate activist Greta Thunberg, attending her first UN climate summit since 2021, said those in power were failing to address the climate crisis. “We are heading toward a future of more genocides and ecocides where basic necessities become luxury,” Thunberg said at a news conference on the sidelines of the summit. “The planet is not dying, it is being killed,” she said. “And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue,” she said.

item.title: Israeli airstrike on Gaza hospital kills 6, injures 20; sparks tensions
item.description: An Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis killed six people, including a doctor, and wounded at least a dozen, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Israeli airstrike on Gaza hospital kills 6, injures 20; sparks tensions

Israeli airstrike on Gaza hospital kills 6, injures 20; sparks tensions An Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis killed six people, including a doctor, and wounded at least a dozen, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

The damage inside Nasser Hospital after an Israeli airstrike in southern Gaza on Thursday | Photo: Reuters

Reuters 1 min read Last Updated : Nov 12 2026 | 11:56 PM IST

Listen to This Article

An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people and wounded at least a dozen more, Gaza's Health Ministry said.   The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck "a senior Hamas terrorist" and other militants, without providing evidence.   The Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgery department and that a doctor was among the dead. An Associated Press journalist at the scene said that parts of the building's second floor were destroyed.   Nasser Hospital in the city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by the war. Israel accuses Hamas and its allies of using hospitals as cover for military activity.

Israeli forces have previously targeted Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.

item.title: Nvidia preparing to oust Jensen Huang after multiple extramarital affairs
item.description: Nvidia Corp.’s board is preparing to oust Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang after multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who is reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy, the ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Lynn Doan Nvidia Corp.’s board is preparing to oust Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang after multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who is reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy, the Wall Street Journal said Wednesday. ALSO READ: Huang said to have had relationship with Nvidia exec who reports to him The board was preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to decide Huang’s fate at the company, the Journal reported, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter. ALSO READ: Alice Huang, alleged Chinese spy in Nvidia scandal, currently in Beijing Nvidia’s board has been facing a succession crisis since Sunday when Huang admitted that he’d had an affair with Alice Huang, who is reportedly suspected of spying on behalf of China. The disclosure shined a light on Nvidia’s lack of a succession plan for Huang and reinforced how inseparable the 63-year-old CEO is from the company and its success. Huang’s potential exit would reverberate far beyond the company’s operations, and not just because Nvidia is the dominant maker of chips at the heart of the AI boom. Huang is a consummate dealmaker and has used the company’s vast resources to invest in the AI supply chain and a variety of startups. He’s also a top evangelist for the AI revolution itself, downplaying fears about the risks to humanity and talking up the benefits. Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Shares of Nvidia dropped 8% in extended trading to $159.95 at about 5:35 p.m. New York time. That’s after closing at $173.73 on Wednesday. Earlier on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, citing unidentified people who worked at the company. Huang and Powell were captured on video being affectionate at a hotel in San Jose, California, during an Nvidia conference in March, according to the Times. Powell didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.  On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm that was spun out of a Chinese gaming enterprise. That data center company, which is Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customer, has been under US investigation for months related to potential chip smuggling, Bloomberg has reported. Megaspeed and Nvidia have denied wrongdoing. Beijing has dismissed allegations that it spied on Huang.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Democrats ready to fight Trump on immigration, but how far can they go?

Democrats ready to fight Trump on immigration, but how far can they go? Democrats plan to use their control of Congress next year to investigate ICE enforcement tactics and push bills expanding pathways to legal status, but Trump's veto power could limit their efforts

Trump's immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability, with his approval on the issue falling to 38% from 50% at the start of his presidency (Photo:PTI)

Reuters 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 12 2026 | 10:30 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Democratic lawmakers are gearing up to fight President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown when in control of Congress next year, targeting ICE tactics and expanding paths to legal status despite limits on how much they can achieve.   Democrats handily won control of both chambers of Congress last week, fueled in part by voters' dissatisfaction with Trump's aggressive arrest and deportation campaign. But lawmakers from both parties expect Stephen Miller, the architect of that campaign and Trump's new chief of staff, to go on driving immigration policy.   House and Senate staffers told Reuters they expect the president to veto any legislation that would curb immigration enforcement or expand pathways to legal residency and citizenship.

Trump's immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability, with his approval on the issue falling to 38% from 50% at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling, and Latino voters swinging sharply back to Democrats in the midterms after tilting Republican in 2024.   In a Friday interview with CBS' "60 Minutes," Trump acknowledged his deportation strategy may have been "too tough." Asked about that by reporters on Monday, Trump responded: "My policy has not changed." Also Read

US Treasury Secy moved to military housing following Iranian threats

Lutnick stalled Trump's crackdown on diversion of Nvidia chips to China

From steel to pharma, Indian firms bet $40 billion on manufacturing in US premium

US, China must stay clear-eyed on AI cooperation, rivalry: Bessent

Republicans block US House effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth

Democrats will have more latitude on oversight. They have already drawn up a list of investigative targets at the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to staffers, including detention center conditions, fatal use of force by federal agents and the 2025 deportation of Venezuelans to a Salvadoran megaprison.

"We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies," US  Representative Bennie Thompson, a Mississippi Democrat and the soon-to-be chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, told Reuters in a statement.   The party also plans to push for greater transparency into how DHS is spending the more than $100 billion allocated by Congress since last year, staffers said, speaking on condition of anonymity.   At a Wednesday press conference at the US Capitol with House members and newly elected representatives from southwestern border states, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals.

"We're not going to be extreme," Cuellar said, nodding to conservative voters across the United States who cast their votes for Democrats.   Asked for a response to this story, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Reuters in a statement: "The Democrats are colossally misreading the electorate if they think the American people want an extremist, anti-American immigration agenda."   The Department of Homeland Security in a statement said claims the agency had been weaponized against Americans were "absurd and false."   The Democratic Party is in a "whole new world when it comes to their immigration agenda," said Sarah Pierce, social policy director at the center-left Third Way think tank.

"They've clearly broken from the policy that we saw under the Biden administration, but they have yet to offer a proactive vision for what immigration should look like."   Democrat Joe Biden, president from 2021 to 2025, initially rolled back some of the restrictive immigration policies of Trump's first four-year term before taking a tougher approach to the border late in his presidency.  REINING IN ICE   Some Democrats emerged from last week's midterm elections ready for battle.   "We will rip ICE apart," Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said while celebrating her triumph in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens during an enforcement surge in January.

US Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Washington state Democrat and the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee's immigration subcommittee, pledged to summon "every single one of these corrupt people that kidnapped and detained and deported and killed people in the streets."   Just the specter of having to testify on Capitol Hill could change the behavior of federal officials, a Democratic congressional staffer said.   In a statement to Reuters, Josh Gottheimer, a moderate Democratic representative from New Jersey, highlighted the ICE Standards Act, which he introduced in March.   "Agents need real training and body cameras," he said. "They need to wear clear identification unless they are on an undercover operation. They must coordinate with state and local law enforcement."

Republicans counter that they have already provided ICE with funding to purchase body cameras and have resisted Democratic attempts to place further guardrails on the agency.   On the campaign trail in 2024, Trump made no secret of his plans for an immigration crackdown. But the tactics of masked, armed federal agents, first in Minneapolis and then across the country, generated widespread outrage.  REFORMING THE SYSTEM   Jose Parra, a former US Senate aide with knowledge of current congressional discussions on immigration, said "voters moved the goal posts" last week, potentially opening the way for some stalled bills to advance.   He pointed to the Dignity Act, a bipartisan bill that would create a path to legal residence for workers while tightening border security and reforming visa programs.

Another bill likely to gain traction, Parra said, is the Dream and Promise Act, which would open a pathway to US citizenship for immigrants who arrived as children, known as "Dreamers."   Despite Gallup polling that shows more than 80% of Americans support a legal pathway for Dreamers, even that legislation might be difficult to advance, according to a senior Senate Republican aide, who said any serious attempt would likely come closer to the next presidential election.   Parra agreed with that assessment, saying Republicans might want to "take that off the table and not let it be a messaging cudgel against them in 2028."

Trump's veto power will likely be an insurmountable barrier to enacting comprehensive immigration reform or clawing back the tens of billions of dollars already appropriated to ICE.   "Congress has ceded so much of its authority and so much of its power to the executive," said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official. "There are real limitations on how much Congress can do."   Still, she said, lawmakers could use funding deadlines and Senate confirmation votes as leverage. And they could pass measures redirecting ICE funding to popular programs like healthcare or school lunches, even if the bills die on Trump's desk.   At Wednesday's press conference, US Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said his party will have to cut deals with Trump, and that members were already discussing how to move forward with a Dreamers bill by the end of 2026.

"Republicans have been saying we will have immigration reform as soon as we have a safe, secure border," Gallego said. "We have that right now."

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
